newsitem.title: JAMAICA: Chiefs of Caricom vow single market, admit Haiti.
newsitem.headline: Chiefs of Caricom vow single market, admit Haiti.

text.p: The 14-member Caribbean Community (Caricom) ended its four-day summit on Friday, having agreed to put a single market in place by 1999 and admit Haiti as its newest member.
Assembled leaders termed the meeting one of the most historic in the association's 24-year history.

Caricom Secretary-General Edwin Carrington, addressing the closing ceremony in the resort of Montego Bay, said the summit had been a "major leap forward." The group's chairman, Jamaican Prime Minister P.J. Patterson, said "new ground has been broken" as a result of the decisions taken.
Twelve of the 14 leaders signed a protocol to allow for the free movement of capital and services and to permit regional firms to set up anywhere within Caricom without restriction.

St. Lucia abstained to allow for national consultations first, while the Bahamas, which is not a member of the present common market, is awaiting the findings of a study on the possible impact of joining.

The region said it was on target to meet its 1999 deadline for a single market, as more than half the member states already permitted the free movement of skilled labor within the region and a common external tariff would be fully in place by the first of next year.

Caricom reversed a four-year policy of restricting membership to smaller states by accepting a 2-month-old application from Haiti. It decided to defer one from the British Virgin Islands until next year.

Haiti has been invited to participate in all Caricom activities, including the two annual summits of heads of government. A technical team will now begin talks in Port-au-Prince on introducing Haiti into the Caricom single market on a phased basis, taking into account economic conditions there.

"Haiti doesn't belong to any (regional) group," Patterson said in explaining Caricom's decision to accept the country's application, "and that's part of the problem in trying to bring Haiti closer to the rest of the region."

A final agreement covering Haiti's admission is expected to be ready for signing when Caricom leaders meet in the first quarter of next year in Grenada. With the admission of Haiti, Caricom more than doubled its population overnight, from six million to 13 million. It now counts among its members the two states, Haiti and Guyana, with the lowest per capita incomes in the region.
The region used the summit to review progress since its May meeting with President Bill Clinton in Barbados and expressed "concern" over subsequent developments in two areas.

Patterson noted that a bill sponsored by the White House to give Caribbean exports parity with those from Mexico contained some conditions that "seem to require" accession to the North American Free Trade Agreement without providing the full benefits of membership.

In addition, he said the U.S. challenge to the European Union's preferential regime for regional banana exports remained a "vexed issue." He said Caricom insisted on being involved in any discussions between Washington and Brussels, as "it is our livelihood which is at stake."

The region welcomed Clinton's decision to name former Chief of Staff Thomas "Mack" McClarty to serve as the White House's point man and special adviser on U.S.-Caribbean relations as a means of ensuring follow-up on the plan of action signed in Barbados.

Caricom has agreed to begin talks with the Central American Common Market later this month on a free trade accord between the two. Similar talks will begin this year with the Andean Pact and the Dominican Republic.
A proposal to negotiate a free trade accord with Cuba has been deferred pending the findings of a study to be presented to the next meeting of the joint Caricom-Cuba commission in December in Havana.
